newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn plans new budget cuts, unions warn of strikes.
newsitem.headline: Bonn plans new budget cuts, unions warn of strikes.

text.p: A German government minister announced plans at the weekend for a second round of welfare cuts just hours after key elements of a first austerity programme received final parliamentary approval on Friday.

Meanwhile industrial unrest loomed as a row flared between unions and employers over cuts in sick pay, a cornerstone of Bonn's bid to boost employment and get its finances in shape in time to qualify for planned European monetary union in 1999.
In addition to sick pay cuts, the three bills passed in cliffhanger votes on Friday cover pension and health reforms as well as a reduction in workers' protection from dismissal.
German health minister Horst Seehofer told Bild am Sonntag newspaper that the decisions taken so far amounted to no more than a "minimal programme."
"We must save much more in the budget, in taxes and in health and pension insurance," Seehofer said.

Separately, Focus magazine quoted Seehofer as saying unemployed people should be required to take on low paid work in farming and catering sectors hitherto done by 500,000 migrant workers from outside the EU.

"Whoever refuses to do that won't get any money from the labour office," Focus quoted Seehofer, a member of the Christian Social Democrats, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, as saying.

News magazine Der Spiegel reported that Bonn planned to save six to seven billion marks ($3.9 to $4.6 billion) through cuts in unemployment benefit, reductions in job creation schemes in eastern Germany and rules requiring the unemployed to accept low-paid work.

Health and pension reforms approved on Friday account for about a third of the 70 billion marks cuts Bonn is seeking for 1997, most of which are now assured. The cuts in sick pay and protection from firing are aimed at cutting firms' costs and promoting employment.
But unions angrily dismissed calls from employers to amend existing wage deals quickly to include the law allowing firms to cut pay by 20 percent during sick leave.
The law takes effect in November and will immediately affect millions of workers in the chemical, construction, banking and retail sectors.
Union officials said most workers in the giant engineering industry had full sick pay enshrined in wage agreements running until end-1998, and warned employers that those deals were sacrosanct.
Walter Riester, deputy chairman of metalworking union IG Metall, told Bild am Sonntag:

"If the employers want to break existing wage agreements, we will take up the dispute on the spot in the factories, particularly the big factories. No one should have any doubts about our determination to fight."
Ursulka Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the DGB trade union federation, said unions would fight if employers sought to renegotiate existing contracts or refuse to renew expiring agreements.
"Next year in particular will see the threat of hard nationwide disputes," Engelen-Kefer told Bild am Sonntag.

The head of the metal employers' association in the Baden-Wuerttemberg region, Dieter Hundt, said existing provisions for full sick pay in wage deals were not binding and that pay cuts could hence take immediate effect in the engineering sector.
Klaus Murmann, head of the Federation of Employer Associations, also said wage bargainers should use "the new possibilities" provided by the legislation as soon as possible. ($1=1.5126 Mark)
